| `Decimal.compare` | -1, 0 or 1. `1.50` and `1.5` are equal. |
| `Decimal.format(value, locale?, options?)` | Text for people, through `Intl.NumberFormat`, keeping the decimal places. |
| `Decimal.toNumber` | A JavaScript number, when exactness no longer matters, such as for a chart. |
| `IsoDuration.toMillis`, `fromMillis` | To and from milliseconds. |
| `IsoDuration.add` | The sum of two. |
| `IsoDuration.format` | A clock text such as `1:30:00`. |

The helpers are only in `types.ts` when the API uses one of the two types. A `BigDecimal` with your own serializer is recognised too, when the serializer writes text and its descriptor is named `BigDecimal` or `java.math.BigDecimal`.

A `Duration` field used to be generated as `string`. It is `IsoDuration` now, so code that assigns plain text to one needs `as IsoDuration`, or better `IsoDuration.fromMillis(...)`.

## Sealed classes

A sealed class or interface becomes a union of its subtypes, each with a literal `type` field, so TypeScript narrows it in a `switch`. The generated companion also lists the type names and has an exhaustive `match`: leave out a case and the code does not compile.

```kotlin
@Serializable
sealed interface Activity

@Serializable
@SerialName("created")
data class Created(val at: Instant) : Activity

@Serializable
@SerialName("archived")
data class Archived(val at: Instant, val title: String) : Activity
```

```ts
import { Activity, api } from '#api';

const lines = (await api.notes.getActivity(id)).map((item) =>
    Activity.match(item, {
        created: (created) => `Created at ${created.at}`,
        archived: (archived) => `Archived "${archived.title}"`
    })
);
```

Use `@SerialName` for short type names. Without it, the type name is the fully qualified class name.

## Getting exact types

Ktor's compiler plugin reads `call.receive<T>()`, `call.respond()` and `call.queryParameters` for you, so plain routes get full types. Add the Ktor Gradle plugin:

```kotlin
plugins {
    id("io.ktor.plugin") version "3.6.1"
}

ktor {
    openApi {
        enabled = true
        codeInferenceEnabled = true
        onlyCommented = false
    }
}
```

Without it, describe routes by hand. A route with no description still gets a service, but it returns `unknown`:

```kotlin
get("/api/todos") { call.respond(todos) }.describe {
    responses {
        HttpStatusCode.OK { schema = jsonSchema<List<Todo>>() }
    }
}
```

Source: https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/playground

# Generator playground

Paste an OpenAPI document and see the TypeScript that `generateTs` writes for it. The playground runs the same generator as the Ktor plugin, compiled to JavaScript, so nothing leaves your browser.

Only paths under the API prefix are kept, as in your app. The document must be JSON, which is what Ktor produces. In a real project the generator also adds the `LucideIcon` type when `lucide` is enabled and `readPublicConfig()` when you set `publicConfig`, so those are missing here. See [Generated TypeScript](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/typescript) for what each file contains and how to use it.

Source: https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/calling-the-api

# Calling the API

Use the generated client from components and load functions, handle typed errors, stream events, page through lists and upload files.

```ts
import { api, apiConfig } from '#api';

const notes = await api.notes.list({ search: 'milk' });
const note = await api.notes.get(1);
await api.notes.update(1, { title: 'Oat milk' });

apiConfig.headers['Authorization'] = 'Bearer token';
```

When several components load the same data at the same time, set `apiConfig.dedupeGets = true`. Identical GET requests that are still in flight then share one network request and get the same parsed result, so do not mutate it. Calls with their own `headers`, `fetch` or `signal` are never shared, and nothing is cached after a response arrives. It is off by default.

## Prefetch on hover

Projects created by ktor-svelte set `data-sveltekit-preload-data="hover"` on `<body>`, so SvelteKit runs a page's `load` function when the pointer rests on a link to it. A `load` that calls the API through `apiWith(event)` therefore fetches its data before the click, and the page opens without waiting. Add the attribute to `src/app.html` in older projects.

For data a component fetches itself, prefetch the call. The next identical GET within 10 seconds gets that response instead of a new request, once:

```svelte
<script lang="ts">
    import { api, prefetchOnHover } from '#api';
</script>

{#each notes as note (note.id)}
    <a href="/notes/{note.id}" use:prefetchOnHover={() => api.notes.get(note.id)}>{note.title}</a>
{/each}
```

`prefetchOnHover` starts after the pointer rests for 50 ms, or at once on focus or touch. Call `prefetch(() => api.notes.get(id))` yourself for other triggers, and pass a second argument to change how long the result is kept, in milliseconds. Only GET requests made synchronously inside the callback are prefetched, without their own `headers` or `signal`, and a failed prefetch is simply forgotten.

Errors are typed too. Ktor's compiler plugin finds error responses such as `call.respond(HttpStatusCode.NotFound, Problem(...))`, and `isApiError` narrows the body:

```ts
import { api, isApiError, isValidationError } from '#api';

try {
    await api.notes.create({ title: '' });
} catch (error) {
    if (isValidationError(error)) showErrors(error.body.fields);
    if (isApiError(error, 'notes.get')) console.log(error.body.message);
}
```

When you only need one line to show, `errorMessage` turns anything a call can throw into text: the `message` of the error body when the server sent one, and otherwise a sentence for a timeout, for a lost connection, or for everything else:

```ts
import { api, errorMessage } from '#api';

let problem = '';

try {
    await api.notes.create({ title: 'Buy milk' });
} catch (error) {
    problem = errorMessage(error);
}
```

To change or translate the three built-in sentences, assign to `errorMessages.network`, `errorMessages.timeout` and `errorMessages.failed` once at startup.

### Error codes

A page that has to tell "this email is taken" from "the last admin cannot leave" should not compare status numbers or message text. Give the errors names, in one enum, and name it in `install(Svelte)`:

```kotlin
enum class AccountError { EmailTaken, LastAdmin }

install(Svelte) {
    generateTs = true
    errorCodes<AccountError>()
}
```

A route answers with a code, either directly or by throwing from anywhere below it:

```kotlin
import io.github.nijasc.ktor.svelte.ApiException
import io.github.nijasc.ktor.svelte.respondError

post("/api/register") {
    call.respondError(AccountError.EmailTaken, HttpStatusCode.Conflict)
}

put("/api/admin/users/{id}/role") {
    throw ApiException(AccountError.LastAdmin, HttpStatusCode.Conflict)
}
```

The answer is `{ "message": "Email taken.", "code": "EmailTaken" }` with the given status, 400 when none is given. The generated client knows the enum as the type `ErrorCode`, so a mistyped or removed code no longer compiles:

```ts
import { api, ErrorCode, hasErrorCode } from '#api';

try {
    await api.register.create(form);
} catch (error) {
    if (hasErrorCode(error, ErrorCode.EmailTaken)) emailProblem = error.body.message;
    else throw error;
}
```

The message is the code's name as a sentence unless you say otherwise. There are three places to say otherwise, and the first that applies wins:

- One answer: `call.respondError(code, status, message = "...")`, or the `message` of `ApiException`.
- Every answer, on the server: `errorCodes<AccountError> { call, code -> ... }` returns the text for a code, or null to leave it. It gets the call, so it can translate.
- In the browser: `setCodeMessages({ EmailTaken: 'That email already has an account.' })` once at startup. `errorMessage`, and so the toasts of `toasts()`, then use this text for the code and ignore what the server sent. A value can be a function, for a translation that depends on the current language.

An app has one enum of error codes. A class of your API named `ErrorCode` clashes with the generated type and stops generation.

### Query parameters as a class

A list route usually reads its query string one parameter at a time, converts each by hand and guesses what to do with a wrong one, and the generated client sees a handful of optional strings. Describe the query as a class instead:

```kotlin
import io.github.nijasc.ktor.svelte.query
import io.github.nijasc.ktor.svelte.queryOf

@Serializable
data class NoteQuery(
    val search: String? = null,
    val status: Status? = null,
    val mine: Boolean = false,
    @JsonSchema.Minimum(1.0) @JsonSchema.Maximum(100.0) val limit: Int = 20,
    val tags: List<String> = emptyList(),
)

get("/api/notes") {
    val query = call.query<NoteQuery>()
    call.respond(notes.find(query))
}.queryOf<NoteQuery>()
```

- `call.query<NoteQuery>()` reads the query string into the class. Numbers, booleans and enums are converted, a parameter that is given several times fills a list, and what is not there takes the property's default.
- A value that does not fit, such as `limit=many` or an unknown status, and a missing parameter without a default, are answered with the same 422 as a request body, with the field named. The `JsonSchema` annotations and `Validated` rules apply too.
- Parameters the class does not have are ignored, and an empty one counts as not given, as a form sends it for an empty field.
- `.queryOf<NoteQuery>()` tells the generated client about the parameters. Without it the function has no `query` argument.

The generated function takes the same fields with their types:

```ts
await api.notes.list({ status: Status.OPEN, mine: true, limit: 50, tags: ['home', 'food'] });
```

The properties can be text, numbers, booleans, enums, value classes over those, types that are written as text such as dates, and lists of them. A nested class is refused when the route is declared.

### Changing some fields

A `PUT` replaces a record, so the browser has to send every field, also the ones the visitor never touched. A `PATCH` sends only what changed, but then the server has to tell a field that was left out from one that was set to null, and a nullable Kotlin property cannot: both arrive as null. `Patch<T>` can, without a second DTO:

```kotlin
import io.github.nijasc.ktor.svelte.Patch

patch("/api/notes/{id}") {
    val patch = call.receive<Patch<NoteInput>>()
    val stored = notes.find(id)
    val updated = patch.applyTo(stored.toInput())
    call.respond(notes.save(id, updated))
}
```

- `applyTo` returns the given object with the sent fields replaced. A field that was not sent keeps its value, and one sent as null becomes null.
- The result is checked like a received object: the bounds from annotations and the `Validated` rules, answered with the usual 422. `@Trim` and the other normalisers apply to the sent fields.
- A field the class does not have, null for a property that is not nullable, or a value of the wrong type is a 400.
- `NoteInput::title in patch`, `patch.has("title")` and `patch.fields` say what was sent, for a route that treats one field specially.

In the generated client the body is the class with every field optional, and null allowed where the class allows it:

```ts
import { api, patchOf } from '#api';

await api.notes.patch(note.id, { dueOn: null });
await api.notes.patch(note.id, patchOf(original, draft));
```

`patchOf(before, after)` is the fields that differ between two objects, with null for the ones that were cleared, so an edit form sends what the visitor changed and nothing else. `applyPatch(target, patch)` does on the client what `applyTo` does on the server, for showing the result before the answer is there. `Patch<T>` is the type of both.

### Two people, one record

Two people open the same record, both change it, both save. Without a check the second save silently replaces the first. With a version, the second one is told.

Give the record a number that changes on every save, a counter or the time of the last change, send it out with the record and take it back with an update:

```kotlin
import io.github.nijasc.ktor.svelte.respondIfStale

@Serializable
data class Note(val id: Int, val title: String, val version: Long)

@Serializable
data class NoteUpdate(val title: String, val version: Long? = null)

put("/api/notes/{id}") {
    val update = call.receive<NoteUpdate>()
    val stored = notes.find(id)
    if (call.respondIfStale(update.version, stored.version) { stored }) return@put
    call.respond(notes.save(id, update))
}
```

When the version that came in is not the stored one, `respondIfStale` answers 409 with the code `version.conflict` and the record as it is now, and returns true. The block that gives the record only runs then. An update without a version is not checked, so make the field required if every client must send it. The third argument is the message, for your own wording or language.

In the browser, `isVersionConflict` recognises the answer and gives you the other person's record:

```ts
import { api, isVersionConflict, type Note } from '#api';

try {
    note = await api.notes.update(note.id, draft, { silent: true });
} catch (error) {
    if (!isVersionConflict<Note>(error)) throw error;
    theirs = error.body.current;
}
```

From there the two usual ways out are one line each. To load their version, show `theirs` and start over. To save yours anyway, set `draft.version = theirs.version` and send again.

[`formState`](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/validation) does the bookkeeping: after a conflict, `form.conflict` holds their record, `form.takeTheirs()` resets the form to it, and `form.keepMine()` takes over their version so the next `form.submit` goes through. Pass `takeTheirs` a value when the form's type is not the record's type.

Errors that `StatusPages` sends are invisible to the compiler plugin, because its handlers are plain lambdas. Declare them once, and they join the typed errors of every API endpoint, unless a route already declares that status itself:

```kotlin
install(StatusPages) {
    exception<NotFoundException> { call, cause -> call.respond(HttpStatusCode.NotFound, Problem(cause.message.orEmpty())) }
}
install(Svelte) {
    errorResponse<Problem>(HttpStatusCode.NotFound, HttpStatusCode.Conflict)
}
```

Routes that declare a `text/event-stream` response, for example through `describe`, become async generators. Each event's `data` is parsed as JSON when possible, and the stream ends when the connection closes or you stop iterating:

```ts
for await (const tick of api.ticks.watch()) console.log(tick);
```

Every endpoint is also exported on its own, named after its group and service, such as `notesList` or `notesGet`. Import those in pages that use only a few endpoints, and the bundler leaves the rest of the client out of that page:

```ts
import { notesGet } from '#api';

const note = await notesGet(1);
```

For paged lists, return `Page<T>` from `io.github.nijasc.ktor.svelte` and read a `cursor` query parameter. `next` is the cursor of the following page, or `null` on the last one:

```kotlin
get("/api/notes/feed") {
    val cursor = call.queryParameters["cursor"]
    val page: Page<Note> = store.page(cursor, limit = 20)
    call.respond(page)
}
```

`pages` turns any such endpoint into an async iterator that fetches one page at a time, typed from the endpoint:

```ts
import { api, pages } from '#api';

for await (const notes of pages(api.notes.getFeed, { limit: '50' })) render(notes);
```

Uploads work with `FormData`. Ktor cannot infer a multipart body from `receiveMultipart`, so describe it once, and the generated function takes `body: FormData`:

```kotlin
post("/api/notes/{id}/attachments") {
    call.receiveMultipart().forEachPart { part -> part.dispose() }
    call.respond(HttpStatusCode.NoContent)
}.describe {
    requestBody { ContentType.MultiPart.FormData() }
}
```

Pass `onUploadProgress` to follow the upload. `fetch` cannot report upload progress, so such a call uses `XMLHttpRequest` instead, with the same headers, errors and `signal` support:

```ts
const form = new FormData();
form.append('file', file);
await api.notes.attachments(id, form, {
    onUploadProgress: ({ loaded, total }) => (progress = total ? loaded / total : 0)
});
```

Uploads count towards `maxApiBodySize`, which is 1 MiB by default, so raise it for routes that accept files.

Service names follow your routes: `GET /notes` is `list`, `GET /notes/{id}` is `get`, `POST` is `create`, `PUT` is `update`, `DELETE` is `delete`, and `POST /notes/{id}/archive` is `archive`. Set `operationId` in `describe` to choose your own. Inside a SvelteKit `load`, use `apiWith(event)`. It is the same client, but every call goes through SvelteKit's `fetch`, which prerendering and client-side navigation need:

```ts
import { apiWith } from '#api';
import type { PageLoad } from './$types';

export const load: PageLoad = async (event) => {
    const api = apiWith(event);
    return { notes: await api.notes.list(), stats: await api.stats.list() };
};
```

In development, ktor-svelte also writes `build/ktor-svelte/routes.json`, which maps every generated service to the Kotlin route that serves it:

```json
"notes.get": { "method": "GET", "path": "/api/notes/{id}", "file": "notes/Routes.kt", "line": 43 }
```

Search it for the operation name you see in the frontend, or let an editor plugin use it to jump from a call to its route. `file` is relative to your source root, and `line` is the line of the route's handler. It lives in `build/` because line numbers change with every edit. When ktor-svelte cannot read a handler's location, the entry has only `method` and `path`.

A `fetch` passed in the options of a single call still wins.

To refresh the files without your dev server, for example in CI, run the task below and check for a diff. It starts your app once, so the app's port must be free.

```bash
./gradlew svelteGenerateTs
```

## In load functions

Inside a SvelteKit `load` function, every call has to go through the `fetch` SvelteKit gives you. `apiWith(event)`, shown above, does that for all calls at once. For a single call, pass `fetch` as the last argument:

```ts
import { api } from '#api';
import type { PageLoad } from './$types';

export const load: PageLoad = async ({ fetch, params }) => {
    const note = await api.notes.get(params.id, { fetch });
    return { note };
};
```

With its own `fetch`, SvelteKit knows which requests a page depends on, reuses a response it already has during hydration, and can rerun the load when you invalidate it. Without it, the call still works, but the browser console warns with `window_fetch_in_load`.

`svelteVerifyLoads` finds the calls that forgot. It reads every `+page.ts`, `+page.js`, `+layout.ts` and `+layout.js`, and fails with the file, the line and the call:

```bash
./gradlew svelteVerifyLoads
```

```text
src/routes/notes/[id]/+page.ts:6  api.notes.get(params.id)  ->  use apiWith(event), or pass { fetch } as the last argument
```

It is not part of `check`. The [lint rule](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/frontend-libraries#lint-rules) `ktor-svelte/fetch-in-load` reports the same thing in the editor.

## Refresh the page after a write

After you create, change or delete something, the lists and details on the page are out of date. Tell the client what to do after a successful write, once, in your root layout, and every page keeps itself current:

```ts
import { refreshAll } from '$app/navigation';
import { apiConfig } from '#api';

apiConfig.onWrite = () => void refreshAll();
```

`onWrite` runs after every POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE that succeeds, and `refreshAll` reruns the `load` functions of the page you are on. Writes that finish together, such as three calls in a `Promise.all`, cause one refresh, not three. A failed write does not trigger it, and neither does a read.

A call that should not refresh the page, such as saving a draft while the user types, opts out:

```ts
await api.notes.update(id, draft, { refresh: false });
```

The client does not import SvelteKit itself, so nothing happens until you set `onWrite`. That also means you can do something else there, such as refreshing only one resource with `invalidate`.

## Fixtures for frontend tests

A frontend test should not need the backend running, and writing its answers by hand goes stale. Record them instead. In development, click through the part of the app you want to test, open the [dev panel](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/guide/dev-workflow) and press **Save fixtures**. You get `api-fixtures.json` with every call the page made and what the server answered:

```json
{
    "recorded": "2026-11-16T12:00:00.000Z",
    "calls": [
        { "method": "GET", "path": "/api/notes?page=1", "status": 200, "response": { "items": [] } },
        { "method": "POST", "path": "/api/notes", "status": 201, "request": { "title": "New" }, "response": { "id": 7 } }
    ]
}
```

In a test, let the client answer from that file:

```ts
import { api, apiConfig, fixtureFetch, type ApiFixtures } from '#api';
import recorded from './api-fixtures.json';

apiConfig.fetch = fixtureFetch(recorded satisfies ApiFixtures);

const page = await api.notes.list({ page: 1 });
```

The calls go through the real generated client, so the test sees typed results, `ApiError` for a recorded 404 and validation errors for a recorded 422, exactly as the app does. A call is matched by its method and its path with the query. When the same call was recorded more than once, such as a list before and after a create, the answers come back in that order, and the last one repeats. A call that was never recorded fails with a message that names it.

Look through the file before you commit it. It holds the bodies as they were sent and received, which can include data you would not put in the repository. Fields marked [`@Sensitive`](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/validation#sensitive-fields), such as a password, are saved as `***`. **Clear** in the panel starts a new recording.

## Ask before a call

A call that deletes something should ask first. `confirmed` asks, and only calls when the answer is yes:

```ts
import { api } from '#api';
import { confirmed } from '#lib/ktor-svelte/confirm.ts';

const deleted = await confirmed('Delete this note?', () => api.notes.delete(id), {
    details: 'It cannot be restored.',
    confirm: 'Delete',
    danger: true
});
```

It resolves to what the call returned, or to `undefined` when the answer was no.

With DaisyUI on, the question is a modal in your theme. While the call runs, both buttons are disabled, so it cannot be sent twice. When it fails, the modal stays open and shows the error's `message`, and the user can try again or cancel. `danger: true` makes the confirm button red and puts the focus on Cancel. Escape cancels.

Without DaisyUI it is the browser's own `confirm`, and a failed call rejects as usual.

`svelteSync` writes the helper to `src/lib/ktor-svelte/confirm.ts` for every project that has generated files. The button labels default to `confirmMessages.confirm` and `confirmMessages.cancel`, which you can set once, such as to your translations.

## Show errors automatically

Turn on toasts in Gradle, and every failed API call shows a short message in the corner of the page, so you don't have to write error handling for the common case:

```kotlin
svelte {
    libraries {
        toasts()
    }
}
```

Run `svelteSync` once. It writes `src/lib/ktor-svelte/toasts.ts` and a `src/hooks.client.ts` that sets `apiConfig.onError`. The message comes from the error body's `message`, such as `Problem("That note does not exist.")`, or reads "Something went wrong (error 500)" with the request ID for server errors. Network failures and timeouts get their own message. With DaisyUI, toasts are DaisyUI alerts in your theme. Otherwise they bring their own small style.

Some errors are left to you, because a toast would be the wrong answer:

- 422 validation errors, which your form shows next to the fields.
- 401, which `apiConfig.onUnauthorized` handles.
- Aborted requests, failed prefetches, and calls made with `silent: true`, such as `api.notes.get(id, { silent: true })`.

The promise still rejects, so you can add handling where you want more. Call `toast('Saved.', { kind: 'success' })` from `#lib/ktor-svelte/toasts.ts` for your own messages, give one a button with `action: { label: 'Undo', run: restore }`, and change the built-in texts through `toastMessages`. Without `toasts()`, `apiConfig.onError` is yours to set, for example to report errors to a monitoring service.

## Toasts from the server

Often the route knows best what to tell the user: that the note was saved, that it was the last free seat, that the export will arrive by mail. Say it there:

```kotlin
import io.github.nijasc.ktor.svelte.ToastKind
import io.github.nijasc.ktor.svelte.toast

post("/api/notes") {
    val note = store.create(call.receive<Note>())
    call.toast("Note saved", ToastKind.Success)
    call.respond(HttpStatusCode.Created, note)
}
```

With `toasts()` on, the browser shows it when the answer arrives, and no component has to know. The kinds are `Info`, `Success`, `Warning` and `Error`. With [i18n](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/frontend-libraries#i18n), pass a message in the visitor's language, such as `call.toast(call.messages.noteSaved())`.

The toast travels in a response header, so the body and its type stay what they are, and it works with any status, also with an error or an empty 204. Call `toast` before you respond. A response carries up to five toasts of up to 500 characters each.

The generated client reads the header on answers from your own origin only, so another server cannot put words into your app. Without `toasts()`, set `apiConfig.onToast = (message, kind) => ...` to show them your way, and nothing is shown until you do. Calls made on the server during SSR do not show toasts.

## Navigation from the server

"Create it, then open it" is the same few lines in every form: wait for the answer, read the ID, call `goto`. The route already knows where to go, so let it say so:

```kotlin
import io.github.nijasc.ktor.svelte.navigateTo

post("/api/notes") {
    val note = store.create(call.receive<Note>())
    call.navigateTo("/notes/${note.id}")
    call.respond(HttpStatusCode.Created, note)
}
```

With [typed routes](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/routes) on, write `call.navigateTo(FrontendRoutes.notesId(note.id))`, and a renamed page cannot leave a stale path behind.

After the call succeeded, the browser opens that page with SvelteKit's `goto`, so it is a client-side navigation and not a reload. The code that awaited the call runs first, so it can still use the result. A failed call navigates nowhere.

With `toasts()` on, this is wired up for you. Without it, add one line to your root layout:

```ts
import { goto } from '$app/navigation';
import { apiConfig } from '#api';

apiConfig.onNavigate = (path) => void goto(path);
```

The path has to be one inside your app: `navigateTo` refuses anything that does not start with a single `/`, and the client ignores such a header as well, and reads it on answers from your own origin only. So the header cannot be used to send a visitor to another site.

## Reload after a deploy

Every API response carries the fingerprint of the frontend build the server runs, in the `X-Ktor-Svelte-Build` header. When a response reports a different build than the first one the page saw, the client calls `apiConfig.onNewBuild`, so you can offer a reload instead of running old code against a new API.

The toasts library has that prompt ready. Turn it on in Gradle and run `svelteSync`:

```kotlin
svelte {
    libraries {
        toasts { reloadPrompt() }
    }
}
```

After a deploy, the next API call shows "A new version is available." with a Reload button. The toast stays until the visitor reloads or closes it, and it shows once, not after every call. Change the texts through `toastMessages.newBuild` and `toastMessages.reload`.

To do something else, set the handler yourself. Your handler wins over the prompt:

```ts
import { apiConfig } from '#api';
import { toast } from '#lib/ktor-svelte/toasts';

apiConfig.onNewBuild = () => {
    toast('We just shipped an update.', { duration: 0, action: { label: 'Reload', run: () => location.reload() } });
};
```

Set `buildHeader = false` in `install(Svelte)` to leave the header out.

## Request IDs

Every call from the generated client sends a fresh `X-Request-Id`. The server keeps it when it is well formed, letters, digits, dots, dashes and underscores up to 128 characters, or generates one, and sends it back in the response. Unhandled errors are logged with it, and `ApiError.requestId` carries it, so a user can quote one ID that support finds in the logs:

```ts
try {
    await api.notes.create(draft);
} catch (error) {
    if (error instanceof ApiError) showError(`Something went wrong. Reference: ${error.requestId}`);
}
```

The ID is available in routes as `call.callId`, and with Ktor's `CallLogging` you can put it into every log line with `callIdMdc("requestId")`. The client only sends the header to its own origin, so it never causes CORS preflights. If you install Ktor's `CallId` yourself, your setup is used. `requestIds = false` turns it off.

## Timeouts

A request that hangs blocks the UI until the browser gives up, which can take minutes. Set a timeout for every call, or for one:

```ts
import { api, apiConfig, isTimeoutError } from '#api';

apiConfig.timeout = 10_000;

try {
    const report = await api.reports.create(input, { timeout: 60_000 });
} catch (error) {
    if (isTimeoutError(error)) showError('The server took too long. Please try again.');
}
```

A per-call `timeout` wins over `apiConfig.timeout`, and your own `signal` still works next to it. Event streams ignore `apiConfig.timeout`, because a live stream is supposed to stay open. Give one its own `timeout` if you want that.

## Retries

A GET that fails because the network dropped, the request timed out, or a proxy answered 502, 503 or 504 often works a moment later. Turn retries on once, and the client tries again by itself:

```ts
import { apiConfig } from '#api';

apiConfig.retry = true;
```

It then makes up to three attempts, waiting 300 ms before the second and 600 ms before the third. Only GET requests are retried, because repeating a write could do the work twice. Every other answer, such as a 404 or a 500, fails at once as before, and `apiConfig.onError` only hears about the last failure.

To change the numbers, pass them instead of `true`. A single call can also set its own, or opt out:

```ts
apiConfig.retry = { attempts: 5, delay: 200, maxDelay: 2000 };

const notes = await api.notes.list({ retry: false });
const report = await api.reports.get(id, { retry: { attempts: 2 } });
```

`delay` doubles after every attempt until it reaches `maxDelay`. A call that is aborted through its `signal` stops waiting at once, and each attempt gets the full `timeout`.

### Rate limits

When the server refuses a call with 429, the error says how long to wait. `isRateLimitError` narrows it, and `retryAfter` is the wait in milliseconds, read from the `Retry-After` header:

```ts
import { api, isRateLimitError } from '#api';

let notice = '';

try {
    await api.notes.create({ title: 'Buy milk' });
} catch (error) {
    if (isRateLimitError(error)) {
        const seconds = Math.ceil((error.retryAfter ?? 60_000) / 1000);
        notice = `Too many requests. Try again in ${seconds} seconds.`;
    }
}
```

With retries on, the client waits and sends the call again by itself, once, when the wait is no longer than `maxDelay`, which is five seconds unless you change it. That also applies to writes: a call the rate limit refused never reached your route, so sending it again cannot do the work twice. A longer wait is not sat out, and the error reaches you at once.

### Writes that are safe to send twice

A `GET` can be repeated without harm. A `POST` cannot: when the answer is lost on the way back, the browser does not know whether the order was placed, and sending it again may place it twice. That is why only `GET` requests are retried above.

An idempotency key removes the doubt. The generated client adds a header, `Idempotency-Key`, with a fresh random value to every write, and uses the same value when it sends that call again. Turn on the server side, and a repeated key is answered with the stored first answer instead of doing the work again:

```kotlin
install(Svelte) {
    idempotency()
}
```

Now a write can be retried, when the call asks for it:

```ts
await api.orders.create(order, { retry: true });
```

- The repeat gets the same status, body and headers as the first answer, plus `Idempotency-Replayed: true`. [Toasts and navigation from the server](#toasts-from-the-server) are repeated with it, since the first ones never arrived.
- An answer with a status of 500 and above is not kept, so the retry does the work. A repeat that arrives while the first is still running is answered with 409 and the code `idempotency.inProgress`, which the client waits for and retries.
- A key counts for one caller (the same `Authorization` and `Cookie` headers), one method and one path. Somebody else sending the same key gets their own result.
- Answers are kept for ten minutes, at most 10,000 of them, in memory: `idempotency { ttl = 30.minutes; maxEntries = 50_000 }`. With several instances of the app behind a load balancer, a repeat only finds the answer on the instance that gave it.
- Streamed answers and answers above 1 MiB are not kept. Reads and routes outside the API prefixes are not looked at.

`retry` in `apiConfig` still applies to reads only. A write is retried when its own call says `retry`, so the decision stays next to the routes where you know the server side is on. To stop sending the header, set `apiConfig.idempotencyKeys = false`.

## The visitor's time zone

The server usually runs in UTC, and the visitor does not. The generated client sends the browser's time zone with every call to your app, and a route reads it as `call.timeZone`:

```kotlin
get("/api/report") {
    val today = java.time.LocalDate.now(call.timeZone)
    call.respondText("Report for $today")
}
```

It is a `java.time.ZoneId`, such as `Europe/Zurich`, taken from the `X-Time-Zone` header. A request without the header, or with a name the JDK does not know, gets `defaultTimeZone` from `install(Svelte)`, which is `UTC` unless you change it. That covers requests the client does not make, such as a plain link to a download.

The header only goes to your own origin, never to a `baseUrl` on another host. To stop sending it, set `apiConfig.sendTimeZone = false`.

## Search as you type

When every keystroke starts a request, an older, slower response can arrive after a newer one and overwrite it. Wrap the call in `latest`, and each call aborts the one before it:

```ts
import { api, isAbortError, latest } from '#api';

const search = latest(api.notes.list);

async function onInput(term: string) {
    try {
        notes = await search({ search: term });
    } catch (error) {
        if (!isAbortError(error)) throw error;
    }
}
```

A superseded call always rejects with an `AbortError`, even when it was cancelled while its body was being read. Your own `signal` still works alongside it.

Source: https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/validation

# Validation

One set of rules for the server and the browser, with errors per field.

Put simple bounds on the properties with Ktor's `JsonSchema` annotations, and any other rule on the class itself by implementing `Validated`. Both run on every `call.receive` of that class, in every route, for nested classes, lists, map values and sealed subtypes too. Receiving a `List` or `Map` of such classes checks every item. When something fails, the route never runs, and the client gets a 422 with an error list per field, in one standard shape that `isValidationError` understands.

```kotlin
import io.ktor.openapi.JsonSchema

@Serializable
data class NoteInput(
    @JsonSchema.MaxLength(80)
    val title: String,
    val body: String = "",
) : Validated {
    override fun Validator.rules() {
        check(::title, title.isNotBlank()) { "A note needs a title." }
    }
}

post("/api/notes") {
    val input = call.receive<NoteInput>()
    call.respond(HttpStatusCode.Created, store.create(input))
}
```

```json
{ "message": "Validation failed", "fields": { "title": ["A note needs a title."] } }
```

| Annotation | Checks | Message |
|---|---|---|
| `@JsonSchema.MinLength(n)`, `@JsonSchema.MaxLength(n)` | Length of a string | `Must be at most 80 characters.` |
| `@JsonSchema.Minimum(x)`, `@JsonSchema.Maximum(x)` | A number, `exclusive = true` for a strict bound | `Must be at least 1.` |
| `@JsonSchema.Pattern(regex)` | A string contains a match | `Must match ^[a-z]+$.` |

The messages for these bounds are English and are the same in the browser and on the server. For another language, or friendlier wording than `Must match ^[a-z]+$.`, write the rule yourself with `check` and your own text.

Errors use the JSON name, with paths such as `lines[1].sku` for nested values, `prices[eur].amount` for map values and `[0].sku` for the items of a received list. `check(::title, ...)` names the field from the property, so renaming it in the IDE keeps the error in sync. If the property has a different `@SerialName`, pass the name as a string instead.

## Cleaning up input

People paste text with spaces around it and type their email address with capitals. Say once, on the field, how it should arrive, and no route cleans up strings by hand:

```kotlin
@Serializable
data class SignUp(
    @Trim @Lowercase
    val email: String,
    @Trim
    @JsonSchema.MinLength(1)
    val name: String,
    @Trim @EmptyAsNull
    val company: String? = null,
)
```

| Annotation | What arrives in the route |
|---|---|
| `@Trim` | The text without whitespace at both ends |
| `@Lowercase` | The text in lowercase, independent of the server's locale |
| `@EmptyAsNull` | `null` when the text is empty, which is what a form sends for a field left blank. The property has to be nullable |

They are applied in that order, so `@Trim @EmptyAsNull` turns a field of only spaces into `null`. This happens when the JSON body is received, before the bounds and your `Validated` rules run, so `@Trim @JsonSchema.MinLength(1)` refuses a name of only spaces without a rule of your own.

On a `List<String>` or a `Map<String, String>` they apply to every item or value. They are found in nested classes, in lists of classes, in sealed subtypes with the default `type` discriminator, and on the property of a value class, so `value class Email(@Trim @Lowercase val value: String)` is clean wherever it is used.

Only JSON request bodies are cleaned up, not query parameters, and the browser does not apply them: `validate()` in the generated TypeScript checks the text as typed. That only matters for a value that is valid after trimming but not before, which the server then accepts.

## Sensitive fields

The development tools show a lot of what travels between browser and server, and some of it should not be shown: a password, a token, an API key. Mark such a field once:

```kotlin
@Serializable
data class Login(
    val email: String,
    @Sensitive
    val password: String,
)
```

From then on the field's value is replaced by `***` wherever ktor-svelte itself displays or stores it:

- in the `curl` command the [dev panel](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/guide/dev-workflow) copies
- in the [fixtures](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/calling-the-api#fixtures-for-frontend-tests) it saves, for request and response bodies
- in browser console output that is forwarded to the dev log
- in the request list and the slow call log, for a query parameter of that name

It works for requests and for responses, in nested classes too, and by the JSON name of the field, so `@SerialName("api_key")` masks `api_key`.

Two things to know. Masking goes by name: once `password` is marked in one class, every field and query parameter called `password` is masked in those places, in any class. So give a sensitive field a telling name, not `value` or `next`. And it changes nothing about your API: the field is received and returned as before. Keeping a value out of a response is still done by not putting it into the response class.

With `generateTs`, the same annotations end up in OpenAPI and in the generated TypeScript, so a form gets the bounds without asking the server, and `validate()` checks a value in the browser with the same messages the server sends. See [Generated TypeScript](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/typescript#generated-typescript).

For a rule that depends on the route, such as comparing against a database, call `validate { check(...) { ... } }` inside the route. It answers the same way. If you use Ktor's `StatusPages` with a handler for all exceptions, it runs first, so let `ValidationException` through.

`use:field` puts the bounds on an input and shows its errors right after it, with `aria-invalid` and `aria-describedby` set for screen readers. Pass the same errors whether they come from `validate()` or from a 422:

```svelte
<input bind:value={draft.title} use:field={{ bounds: NoteInput.bounds.title, errors: errors.title, errorClass: 'text-error' }} />
```

The message is a `<p role="alert">` with the class `field-error` unless you pass `errorClass`, and it disappears when the errors are empty. If the input has a hint of its own, pass the hint's id as `describedBy`, and it stays in `aria-describedby` next to the error.

With `libraries { components() }`, the generated [`<Field>`](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/frontend-libraries#field) wraps this action together with the label and a hint.

## Form state

Every form needs the same few variables: the values being edited, whether they changed, whether a submit is running, and the errors that came back. `formState` holds them, so a form is its inputs and one function:

```svelte
<script lang="ts">
    import { api, field, NoteInput } from '#api';
    import { formState } from '#lib/api/form-state.svelte.ts';

    const form = formState<NoteInput>(NoteInput.empty(), { validate: NoteInput.validate, resetOnSuccess: true });

    async function create() {
        const note = await form.submit((draft) => api.notes.create(draft));
        if (note) console.log('created', note.id);
    }
</script>

<form onsubmit={(event) => { event.preventDefault(); void create(); }}>
    <input bind:value={form.draft.title} use:field={{ bounds: NoteInput.bounds.title, errors: form.errors.title }} />
    <p role="alert">{form.message}</p>
    <button disabled={form.submitting}>Create</button>
    <button type="button" disabled={!form.dirty} onclick={() => form.reset()}>Discard</button>
</form>
```

| | |
|---|---|
| `form.draft` | The values being edited, deeply reactive, so `bind:value={form.draft.title}` works |
| `form.dirty` | `true` while the draft differs from the last saved values |
| `form.submitting` | `true` while `submit` waits for the server. A second `submit` in that time does nothing |
| `form.errors` | Errors per field, from `validate` or from a 422 answer. Hand them to `use:field` |
| `form.error`, `form.message` | Any other failure of the last submit, and its text for the user. `message` is empty when there is none |
| `form.reset()` | Back to the last saved values, with the errors cleared. `form.reset(values)` makes `values` the saved ones, such as after loading a record |
| `form.submit(send)` | Runs `validate` first and stops on errors without calling the server. Otherwise calls `send` with a plain copy of the draft and returns its result, or `undefined` when it failed |

After a successful submit the sent values are the saved ones, so the form is no longer dirty. That suits an edit form. For a form that creates something, `resetOnSuccess: true` empties it again.

`submit` never throws: a failed call ends up in `errors` or `error`. The failure still reaches `apiConfig.onError`, so with [toasts](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/calling-the-api#show-errors-automatically) on, the user sees it without any markup of yours.

The helper uses runes, so it is a module of its own and not part of `#api`. The draft should be plain data, the kind that goes into a JSON body. `dirty` compares it as JSON.

## Checks only the server can make

Whether an email address is taken, or a coupon code exists, cannot be decided in the browser. Without help, the visitor learns it after sending the whole form. A check route answers the question for one value:

```kotlin
import io.github.nijasc.ktor.svelte.fieldCheck

routing {
    fieldCheck("/api/checks/email") { email ->
        if (email == "ada@example.com") "That email address already has an account." else null
    }
}
```

The block gets the value and returns what is wrong with it, or null when it is fine. It runs inside the route, so `call` is there for the current user or the language. The route is a `GET` with the value in the query, never cached, and part of the generated client like any other.

`formState` asks it while the visitor types:

```svelte
<script lang="ts">
    import { api, field, Registration } from '#api';
    import { formState } from '#lib/api/form-state.svelte.ts';

    const form = formState<Registration>(Registration.empty(), {
        validate: Registration.validate,
        checks: { email: api.checks.getEmail }
    });
</script>

<input type="email" bind:value={form.draft.email} use:field={{ errors: form.errors.email }} />
```

- The call waits until typing has paused for 300 ms (`checkDelay`), and an answer that arrives for an older value is dropped.
- The answer is part of `form.errors.email`, next to the errors from `validate` and from a 422, so it shows up the same way with no extra markup.
- While a check says no, `form.submit` does not send. `form.checking` is true while an answer is awaited.
- An empty value and the value the form started with are not checked. A profile form does not tell its owner that their own email is taken.
- A check that fails, because the server is unreachable or answers with an error, says nothing. The real answer comes when the form is sent.

A check does not replace the rule in the route that saves: two people can pass the check at the same moment. Keep the rule there and treat the check as the earlier, friendlier message.

A check route also tells anyone who asks whether a value exists. For email addresses that reveals who has an account, so put the route under a [rate limit](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/calling-the-api#rate-limits), as you would the sign-in route.

Source: https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/transport

# Transport and compression

JSON, XML and other formats, and compressed API responses.

Choose how your API talks inside `install(Svelte)`. Without a `transport` block, nothing is installed and you stay in control.

```kotlin
install(Svelte) {
    transport {
        json { prettyPrint = true }
        xml()
        compression()
    }
}
```

| Function | Effect |
|---|---|
| `json()` | Adds JSON to Ktor's `ContentNegotiation`. Takes a `kotlinx.serialization` `Json` builder |
| `xml()` | Adds XML. Needs `implementation("io.ktor:ktor-serialization-kotlinx-xml")` in your build |
| `negotiation { }` | Registers any other format, such as CBOR, on `ContentNegotiation` directly |
| `compression { }` | Installs Ktor's `Compression`. Takes its normal configuration, and defaults to gzip and deflate |

The client picks a format with its `Accept` header, and the first format you list is the default. Already installing these plugins yourself? You will get a clear error at startup, so remove one of the two. Files precompressed by your adapter are left alone. The generated TypeScript client always speaks JSON.

## API compression

API responses are compressed by default, without any `transport` block. Responses of 1 KiB or more on your API paths with a JSON, XML, CBOR or text content type are sent with gzip or deflate, whichever the client prefers. Browsers decompress them natively, so the generated client and DevTools see plain JSON, and clients that send no `Accept-Encoding`, such as curl, get plain JSON too. Server-sent events, small responses, other content types and frontend files are left alone, and request bodies are never decompressed.

Add Ktor's zstd module, and current browsers get zstd instead, which compresses about as well as gzip at a fraction of the CPU time:

```kotlin
implementation("io.ktor:ktor-server-compression-zstd:<ktor version>")
```

It adds a native library of about 7 MB to your JAR, which is why it is not included by default.

Compression and secrets: a response that contains a secret, such as an API key, next to text an attacker can choose can leak that secret byte by byte through its compressed size (the BREACH attack). ktor-svelte's own CSRF protection uses no tokens, so it is not affected. If one of your endpoints returns such a mix, turn `apiCompression` off or install `Compression` yourself with a condition that skips that route.

If you install `Compression` yourself, before or after `install(Svelte)`, or use `transport { compression() }`, your configuration is used instead. To send API responses uncompressed:

```kotlin
install(Svelte) {
    apiCompression = false
}
```

Why compression and not a binary format: for 5000 notes, gzip cut the time from server to parsed data from 318 ms to 152 ms on a 50 Mbit connection and from 1537 ms to 381 ms on 4G, and zstd to 84 ms and 345 ms. CBOR was 7 percent smaller than JSON before compression and larger after it, and decoding it in JavaScript took about seven times as long as `JSON.parse`, so it never came out ahead.

Source: https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/auth

# Auth

Use Ktor authentication with the generated client.

To put the frontend behind Ktor's authentication, take over its routing. List what stays public. Those paths must include your login page and `/_app/*`, or the login page cannot load. Anyone can still download the JS bundles under `/_app`, so keep secrets on the server.

```kotlin
install(Svelte) {
    routing = SvelteRouting.Manual
}

routing {
    svelte(public = listOf("/login", "/_app/*"))
    authenticate("session") {
        svelte()
    }
}
```

Pages served by a plain `svelte()` get `private` caching, so shared proxies do not keep them. Paths in the `public` list keep normal caching.

In the browser, react to expired sessions in one place:

```ts
apiConfig.onUnauthorized = () => goto('/login');
```

In development mode, `svelte(public = ...)` also opens the paths Vite needs, so hot reload works on your login page.

Source: https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/runtime-config

# Runtime config

Pass values to the frontend at startup, so one JAR works in every environment. The type comes along with `generateTs`:

```kotlin
@Serializable
data class AppConfig(val sentryDsn: String?)

install(Svelte) {
    publicConfig(AppConfig(sentryDsn = System.getenv("SENTRY_DSN")))
}
```

```ts
import { loadPublicConfig } from '#api';

const config = await loadPublicConfig();
```

The config is also inlined into every page as `<script type="application/json" id="ktor-svelte-config">`, so it is there before your code runs, without a request. Read it synchronously, for example in a store or a component's script:

```ts
import { readPublicConfig } from '#api';

const config = readPublicConfig();
```

`loadPublicConfig()` uses the inlined copy when it is there and only asks the server otherwise, which is the case during development with Vite. The JSON is escaped, so a value cannot close the script tag. Pages with the config are prepared once and cached, with their own ETag and a gzip copy. Set `inlinePublicConfig = false` to keep the config out of pages.

## Changing values without a restart

Pass a function instead of a value when the config comes from somewhere you edit while the app runs, such as a file:

```kotlin
install(Svelte) {
    publicConfig { Json.decodeFromString<AppConfig>(Path("config/public.json").readText()) }
}
```

In development the function runs on every request for the config and for every page, so a saved change shows up on the next page load. Inlined pages get a new ETag when the config changes, so the browser does not keep a stale copy. In production the function runs once at startup and the result is kept, so a broken file fails the start instead of a request.

## Keep secrets out

It is served as JSON from `/_ktor-svelte/config.json` to anyone who asks, so **never put secrets in it**. In SvelteKit, call `loadPublicConfig` only in the browser, because prerendering has no server to ask.

## Trying other values in development

To see the frontend with another value, you do not have to change the config: the [dev panel](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/guide/dev-workflow) can override `publicConfig` values for your browser only.

## Environment variables

An app that reads `System.getenv` here and there finds out one variable at a time what is missing, in production, and nobody knows the full list. Declare them in one place instead:

```kotlin
import io.github.nijasc.ktor.svelte.EnvironmentScope
import io.github.nijasc.ktor.svelte.environment

class AppEnvironment(env: EnvironmentScope) {
    val databaseUrl = env.string("DATABASE_URL", "JDBC URL of the database", example = "jdbc:postgresql://localhost/app")
    val port = env.int("PORT", "Port the server listens on", default = 8080)
    val signKey = env.secret("SESSION_SIGN_KEY", "Signs the session cookie")
    val siteUrl = env.optional("SITE_URL", "Public address, for links in emails")
    val signUps = env.oneOf<SignUps>("SIGN_UPS", "Whether new people can register", default = SignUps.Open)
}

fun main() {
    val env = environment(declare = ::AppEnvironment)
    embeddedServer(Netty, port = env.port) { module(env) }.start(wait = true)
}
```

`environment` reads every variable, converts it, and returns your class with typed values. When something is missing or does not fit, the app stops before it does anything else, with all of it in one table:

```text
The app cannot start: 2 environment variables are missing or wrong.

  DATABASE_URL  missing                         JDBC URL of the database, such as jdbc:postgresql://localhost/app
  PORT          "eighty" is not a whole number  Port the server listens on

Set them in the environment. .env.example lists every variable the app reads.
```

| Function | Value |
|---|---|
| `string(name, description, default?, example?)` | Text. Required unless it has a default. |
| `optional(name, description, example?)` | Text or null. |
| `secret(name, description)`, `optionalSecret(...)` | Text that must not be shown. Its value never appears in the example file or in messages. |
| `int(name, description, default?, example?)` | A whole number. |
| `boolean(name, description, default?)` | `true` or `false`. |
| `oneOf<E>(name, description, default?)` | One of the values of an enum, in any letter case. |

An empty variable counts as not set.

### .env.example

`svelteGenerateTs` writes `.env.example` next to `build.gradle.kts` from the same declaration, and dev mode keeps it current. Each variable is there with its description, whether it is required, and its default or example. Secrets are listed without a value. `svelteVerifyTs`, and so `check`, fails when the file is out of date, so a new variable cannot be added without it showing up in a pull request.

The generating run starts the app without your environment. It therefore does not stop for missing variables: a required one reads as its example, or as empty text. Code that runs at startup, such as connecting to the database, should already be skipped in that run or tolerate that, as it must today for `svelteGenerateTs` to work on a build server.

## Secrets in the frontend build

Everything in the frontend build is sent to browsers. A secret gets in there easily: a server-only variable imported in a component, a key pasted into a config file, a `.env` value Vite was told to expose. Nothing fails, and the key is public from the next deploy on.

`svelteVerifyLeaks` runs after `svelteBuild`, before the build is packed into the JAR, and looks for secret values in the built files. When it finds one, the build fails:

```text
ktor-svelte found secret values in the frontend build. Everything in that folder is sent to browsers.

  SESSION_SIGN_KEY (declared as a secret)  _app/immutable/chunks/B3kq9.js
  STRIPE_KEY (.env)                        _app/immutable/nodes/2.Dx1.js

Read such values on the server only. A value that is meant to be public belongs in svelte { buildEnv }, or gets a name that starts with PUBLIC_.
```

It names the variable and the file, never the value. The values it looks for are:

- the [declared environment variables](#environment-variables) marked as `secret`, with the value they have in the environment of the build
- every value in `.env`, `.env.local`, `.env.production` and `.env.production.local`, next to `build.gradle.kts` and in the frontend folder

Left out are variables listed in `buildEnv`, names that start with `PUBLIC_` or `VITE_`, values shorter than eight characters, and values that are one plain word, such as `production`. Those would be found in almost any build.

The check can only find a secret whose value it knows. On a build server that does not have the production secrets, it has nothing to compare, which is one more reason to build with the real environment or not at all. To turn it off:

```kotlin
svelte {
    verifyLeaks = false
}
```

Source: https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/endpoints

# Built-in endpoints

The status and health endpoints and Swagger UI, all off by default.

## Sitemap and robots.txt

Search engines find your pages through `/sitemap.xml` and read `/robots.txt` first. ktor-svelte serves both for you when your build has neither:

- `/sitemap.xml` lists every prerendered page in the build, so `about.html` becomes `/about` and `docs/index.html` becomes `/docs/`. The SPA fallback and the 404 page are left out.
- `/robots.txt` lets crawlers read all pages, keeps them out of your API prefixes and `/_ktor-svelte/`, and points to the sitemap.

Pages that only exist at runtime, such as `/notes/42`, can't be listed, because there is no file for them. URLs in both files must be absolute, so set the public address of your site. Otherwise it is taken from the request, which behind a proxy needs Ktor's `ForwardedHeaders` or `XForwardedHeaders` plugin:

```kotlin
install(Svelte) {
    siteUrl = "https://example.com"
}
```

To write your own, put `sitemap.xml` or `robots.txt` in `frontend/static/`. Files from the build always win. `sitemap = false` turns both off. With `routing = SvelteRouting.Manual`, they are only served where you route `svelte()`.

## Default favicon

Browsers ask every site for `/favicon.ico`. Until your app has its own icon, ktor-svelte answers with a ktor-svelte one, so tabs and bookmarks show something and the log has no 404s for it. It serves `/favicon.ico`, `/favicon.svg`, `/favicon.png` and `/apple-touch-icon.png`, cached for a day.

As soon as your build has any of `favicon.ico`, `favicon.svg` or `favicon.png`, for example in `frontend/static/`, none of the defaults are served and yours are used. In development, ktor-svelte checks `frontend/static/` instead. Turn the default off with `defaultFavicon = false`.

## Status endpoint

```kotlin
install(Svelte) {
    statusEndpoint = true
}
```

`GET /_ktor-svelte/status` returns JSON with the bundled build (`present`, `formatVersion`, `files`, `fingerprint`) and the dev proxy (`proxy`, and when active `url` and `reachable`), and how many requests the security guards refused (`refusals`: `crossOrigin`, `bodyTooLarge`, `rateLimit`). It is off by default, never cached, hidden from the OpenAPI document, and answers only requests from this machine with a local `Host`. Everything else gets 403, unless you [open it to more callers](#who-may-see-internal-endpoints).

## Health endpoint

For load balancers, container orchestrators and uptime checks:

```kotlin
install(Svelte) {
    healthEndpoint = true
    healthCheck { database.isReachable() }
}
```

`GET /_ktor-svelte/health` answers `200` with `{"status":"up"}` when the frontend can be served and every `healthCheck` returns `true`, and `503` with `{"status":"down"}` otherwise. A check that throws counts as down and is logged. Unlike the status endpoint, it answers every client, because it reveals nothing beyond up or down. It is off by default, never cached and hidden from the OpenAPI document.

## API docs

`apiDocs = true` serves Swagger UI at `/api/docs` in development mode only, using the same OpenAPI document as `generateTs`. Change the path with `apiDocsPath`. The page loads its scripts from a public CDN, so it needs internet access.

To have the docs on a deployed app as well, say [who may see them](#who-may-see-internal-endpoints). Without that they stay a development tool.

## Who may see internal endpoints

The status endpoint and the API docs are for you and your tools, not for visitors. By default the status endpoint answers this machine only, and the docs exist in development only. One block opens both to the callers you name, and to nobody else:

```kotlin
import io.ktor.server.sessions.get
import io.ktor.server.sessions.sessions

install(Svelte) {
    statusEndpoint = true
    apiDocs = true
    internalAccess {
        token = env("INTERNAL_TOKEN")
        networks("10.0.0.0/8", "fd00::/8")
        allow { call -> call.sessions.get<UserSession>()?.userId == "admin" }
    }
}
```

A request gets in when any one of them lets it in. Requests from this machine always do.

| Setting | Lets in | Good for |
|---|---|---|
| `token` | Requests with `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. At least 16 characters, compared in constant time | A monitoring job that reads the status endpoint |
| `networks(...)` | Clients whose address is in one of the ranges, IPv4 or IPv6 | An office network or a VPN |
| `allow { call -> ... }` | Whatever your own check accepts, such as a signed-in user with a role | Opening the API docs in a browser, which cannot send a token |

With `internalAccess` set, `apiDocs = true` serves the docs outside development too, behind the same rules. Everyone else gets 403, or 401 when a token is configured and none was sent. The app does not start with a token that is too short or a range it cannot read.

Behind a reverse proxy, every request reaches the app from the proxy's address, which is usually a private one. A network range would then let the whole internet in, so ktor-svelte refuses it: when a request carries `X-Forwarded-For` or `Forwarded` and the app has not told Ktor to trust the proxy, `networks` lets nobody in. Install Ktor's `XForwardedHeaders` or `ForwardedHeaders` plugin, and the range is checked against the client's real address.

The health endpoint and the public build info stay open, since they are made for callers you do not know.

Source: https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/frontend-libraries

# Frontend libraries

Tailwind, DaisyUI, Lucide, i18n, image optimization, error toasts and typed routes, configured in Gradle with typed helpers on both sides.

Turn on what you need in `build.gradle.kts`. Packages get installed and configured for you, and everything works together, including across Kotlin and TypeScript.

```kotlin
import io.github.nijasc.ktor.svelte.gradle.DaisyTheme
import io.github.nijasc.ktor.svelte.gradle.LocaleStrategy

svelte {
    libraries {
        tailwind {
            typography()
            forms()
        }
        daisyUi {
            themes(DaisyTheme.ShadcnLight, DaisyTheme.ShadcnDark, DaisyTheme.Cupcake)
            customTheme("brand") {
                primary = "#7f52ff"
                base100 = "#fdfcff"
            }
            defaultTheme(DaisyTheme.ShadcnLight)
            prefersDark(DaisyTheme.ShadcnDark)
        }
        fonts("Inter")
        charts()
        lucide()
        images()
        toasts()
        routes()
        components()
        i18n {
            locales("en", "de")
            defaultLocale = "en"
            strategy = LocaleStrategy.Cookie
        }
    }
}
```

Then apply it:

```bash
./gradlew svelteSync
```

`svelteSync` adds the packages, updates your lockfile and writes the generated files. Commit the result. The generated folder `src/lib/ktor-svelte` carries its own `.gitattributes`, which marks the files as generated and keeps their line endings the same on every machine. `svelteDev` and `svelteDevAll` sync automatically. A production build never changes anything: it fails and asks you to run `svelteSync` if something is out of date.

**ktor-svelte owns `vite.config.ts`** once any library is on. Put your own Vite settings in `vite.user.ts`, and they are merged in:

```ts
export default {
    server: { port: 3000 }
};
```

It also generates `src/hooks.server.ts`, and `src/hooks.ts` for URL prefixes. If you already have your own versions of these files, sync stops rather than overwriting them. It tells you to move your settings and delete the file. To combine your own `handle` with ours, use `sequence` from `@sveltejs/kit/hooks` with `ktorSvelteHandle` from `#lib/ktor-svelte/server-hooks.js`, after removing the generated hook file and any use of a library that needs it.

If you already have `src/routes/+layout.svelte`, add this line once. Without a layout, one is created for you.

```ts
import '#lib/ktor-svelte/app.css';
```

Generated Kotlin lands in the `io.github.nijasc.ktorsvelte` package. Change it with `generatedPackage = "com.example.ui"`.

## Tailwind

`tailwind()` installs Tailwind 4 and wires Vite and the CSS. `typography()` and `forms()` add the official plugins. Everything else is normal Tailwind CSS.

## DaisyUI

Use the theme selector in the top bar of this site to see every theme ktor-svelte ships, the shadcn themes included, applied to these pages. `daisyUi()` turns on Tailwind as well. With no themes listed, you get `Light` and `Dark`. Themes are typed on both sides, and the saved choice is applied before the first paint, so there is no flash of the wrong theme.

```svelte
<script lang="ts">
    import { setTheme, themes } from '#theme';
</script>

{#each themes as theme}
    <button class="btn" onclick={() => setTheme(theme)}>{theme}</button>
{/each}
```

```kotlin
import io.github.nijasc.ktorsvelte.AppTheme
import io.github.nijasc.ktorsvelte.theme

get("/api/report") {
    val isDark = call.theme == AppTheme.Dark
}
```

### shadcn themes

`DaisyTheme.ShadcnLight` and `DaisyTheme.ShadcnDark` bring the look of [shadcn/ui](https://ui.shadcn.com) to every DaisyUI component: its neutral palette, `0.625rem` corners, thin borders and flat surfaces without shadows or noise. Use them like any other theme. Projects created by the setup script start with them:

```kotlin
import io.github.nijasc.ktor.svelte.gradle.DaisyTheme

svelte {
    libraries {
        daisyUi {
            themes(DaisyTheme.ShadcnLight, DaisyTheme.ShadcnDark)
            defaultTheme(DaisyTheme.ShadcnLight)
            prefersDark(DaisyTheme.ShadcnDark)
        }
    }
}
```

On the server they are `AppTheme.ShadcnLight` and `AppTheme.ShadcnDark`, and in the frontend `'shadcn-light'` and `'shadcn-dark'`. When you only pick these two, the dark one is used for visitors who prefer dark mode. Themes appear in `themes` in the order you list them.

`customTheme` also accepts `secondary`, `accent`, `neutral`, `base200`, `base300`, `baseContent`, `info`, `success`, `warning` and `error`, plus `variable("radius-box", "1rem")` for anything else Daisy supports. Pass `colorScheme = "dark"` for dark themes.

You do not have to guess those colors in the build file. With DaisyUI on, the [dev panel](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/guide/dev-workflow) has a **Theme colors** section with a color picker for each of the twelve. Changing one recolors the open page at once, so you tune the theme on your real screens. **Copy for Gradle** puts the result on the clipboard as a finished block, named as you typed it:

```kotlin
customTheme("sunset") {
    primary = "#ff0044"
    secondary = "#f5f5f5"
    base100 = "#fff8e7"
}
```

The real block lists all twelve colors, and says `colorScheme = "dark"` when you started from a dark theme. Paste it into `daisyUi { }`, add the name to your themes, and `svelteSync` makes it a theme like any other. The changes on the page are a preview only: **Reset**, or a reload, brings the theme back.

The saved theme is applied by a small inline script. The automatic [Content-Security-Policy](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/security#security-headers) allows it by its hash. If you set your own `contentSecurityPolicy`, allow it with SvelteKit's `csp` option in `hash` mode.

## Fonts

A font from a font CDN is a request to another company on every first visit, a line in the privacy policy, and an exception in the Content-Security-Policy. `fonts` serves the font from your own app instead:

```kotlin
svelte {
    libraries {
        tailwind()
        fonts("Inter")
    }
}
```

`svelteSync` then does three things:

- It installs the font from [Fontsource](https://fontsource.org), an npm package per font, so the lockfile pins the files like any other dependency.
- It imports the font into the generated stylesheet and makes it the default: `font-sans` in Tailwind, and so the font of the whole page.
- It preloads the Latin file on every page, through the generated server hooks, so text does not first appear in a fallback font.

The files end up in the frontend build under hashed names and are served by your app, with the long cache lifetime of every other asset.

```kotlin
fonts("Inter") {
    mono = "JetBrains Mono"
}
```

`mono` sets the font for code, `font-mono`. Write the names as the fonts are called, with spaces. The font is taken in its variable version, one file for all weights. For a font that has none, say so, and the regular and bold files are used:

```kotlin
fonts("Roboto") {
    variable = false
}
```

`fonts` needs `tailwind()` or `daisyUi()`, which bring the stylesheet. Whether a font exists, and whether it has a variable version, shows on its Fontsource page. A name that does not exist fails at `svelteSync`, when the package cannot be installed. When you drop or change a font, remove its old `@fontsource` package from `package.json` yourself: the plugin does not know which of them are yours.

## Charts

`charts()` sets up [LayerChart](https://layerchart.com), a chart library for Svelte 5, so that its charts take the colors of your DaisyUI themes, light and dark, without any setup of your own:

```kotlin
svelte {
    libraries {
        daisyUi()
        charts()
    }
}
```

`svelteSync` installs the package, adds LayerChart's DaisyUI preset to the generated stylesheet, and writes a small helper for series. A chart is then a component in an element with a height:

```svelte
<script lang="ts">
    import { BarChart, LineChart } from 'layerchart';
    import { chartSeries } from '#charts';

    interface Day {
        day: string;
        opened: number;
        closed: number;
    }

    let { days }: { days: Day[] } = $props();

    const series = chartSeries<Day>({ opened: 'Opened', closed: { label: 'Closed', color: 'success' } });
</script>

<div class="h-64">
    <LineChart data={days} x="day" {series} />
</div>
```

`chartSeries<Day>` is the typed part. Its keys must be number properties of `Day`, so a renamed field fails `svelteCheck` instead of drawing an empty chart. Each entry is a label, or a label and one of the theme's colors: `primary`, `secondary`, `accent`, `neutral`, `info`, `success`, `warning` and `error`. Without a color, the series take them in that order. The colors are CSS variables, so a chart follows the theme when the visitor switches it.

`chartColors` holds the same colors, for anything else you draw. For what the components can do, see LayerChart's own documentation. `charts()` needs `daisyUi()`.

## Lucide

`lucide()` generates a `LucideIcon` enum from the installed version, so a misspelled icon is a compile error. Use it in your DTOs and it reaches the frontend as the same type:

```kotlin
import io.github.nijasc.ktorsvelte.LucideIcon

@Serializable
data class Note(val title: String, val icon: LucideIcon)
```

```svelte
<script lang="ts">
    import Icon from '#icon';
</script>

<Icon name="ArrowRight" size={20} />
<Icon name={note.icon} class="text-primary" />
```

Each icon loads on demand, so you only download the ones a page uses. An icon's enum name is its Lucide name in PascalCase, such as `arrow-right` to `ArrowRight`. Names starting with a digit get an `Icon` prefix. A misspelled icon name from a client gets a 400 from Ktor.

Only the icons your app uses are built into the frontend. `svelteSync` finds them in your Kotlin code (`LucideIcon.Flame`) and in your frontend (`name="ArrowRight"`, `Icon.Tags`, or a string such as `'Search'`), and writes just those into `src/lib/ktor-svelte/icons.ts`. Lucide has almost 2,000 icons, and each would otherwise become its own file in your JAR. In the notes example, this takes the frontend build from 6,180 files and 11 MB down to 120 files and 1.8 MB. The `LucideIcon` enum and the TypeScript type still list every icon, so anything stored or sent stays valid.

In development, an icon that isn't in the list yet still shows, with a console hint to run `svelteSync`. A production build checks the list and fails with "Run svelteSync" when an icon is missing, so nothing silently disappears. `svelteDevAll` syncs on every Kotlin change.

If icon names come from somewhere the scan can't see, such as a database your users fill or an icon picker, keep all icons:

```kotlin
svelte {
    libraries {
        lucide {
            allIcons()
        }
    }
}
```

## Images

`images()` adds SvelteKit's [`@sveltejs/enhanced-img`](https://svelte.dev/docs/kit/images#sveltejs-enhanced-img). Keep pictures next to your code, for example in `frontend/src/lib/assets`, and use `enhanced:img` instead of `img`:

```svelte
<enhanced:img src="#lib/assets/hero.png" alt="Our team" sizes="(min-width: 768px) 65ch, 100vw" />
```

At build time, every image becomes AVIF and WebP in several widths, plus a fallback in the original format, inside a `<picture>` with `srcset`, `width` and `height`. Browsers download only the size and format they need, and the layout doesn't jump while the image loads. In the notes example, a 339 KB PNG becomes an 8 KB AVIF for a laptop screen. The files land in `_app/immutable/`, so browsers cache them for a year like any other hashed asset.

Files in `frontend/static/` are copied as they are, because nothing in the build knows where they are used. Move images there to `src/lib/assets` to have them optimized. Processing uses `sharp`, which comes with prebuilt binaries for Windows, macOS and Linux. The first build with many large images takes longer, and later builds reuse Vite's cache.

## Toasts

`toasts()` shows failed API calls as toasts, without any error handling in your components. See [Show errors automatically](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/calling-the-api#show-errors-automatically).

`toasts { reloadPrompt() }` also offers a reload when the server runs a newer build than the page. See [Reload after a deploy](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/calling-the-api#reload-after-a-deploy).

## Routes

`routes()` turns every page into a typed constant in TypeScript and Kotlin, for links and redirects that always point to a real page. See [Typed routes](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/routes).

## i18n

Keep one JSON file per language in `frontend/messages`. Change the folder with `messagesDir`. `svelteInit` creates an empty file for every locale you configured, and never touches one that is already there. Files are flat, and `{name}` is a parameter:

```json
{
  "server-greeting": "Hello {name}, greetings from Ktor!",
  "app-title": "Notes"
}
```

Both sides get typed functions from the same files. A missing key or a mismatched parameter in any language fails the build, so translations can't drift.

While `svelteDevAll` or `svelteDev` runs, saving a message file updates the frontend functions at once, and Vite reloads them, with no Gradle run. Under `svelteDevAll` the Kotlin `Messages` follow and the app restarts. With `svelteDev` alone, they update the next time Kotlin compiles. A file with a missing key or a mismatched parameter is reported in the console, and the last good version stays until you fix it.

```svelte
<script lang="ts">
    import { getLocale, localizeHref, locales, m, setLocale } from '#i18n';
</script>

<h1>{m.appTitle()}</h1>
<p>{m.serverGreeting({ name: 'Ada' })}</p>
<a href={localizeHref('/about')}>About</a>
<button onclick={() => setLocale('de')}>Deutsch</button>
```

```kotlin
import io.github.nijasc.ktorsvelte.Messages
import io.github.nijasc.ktorsvelte.messages

get("/api/hello") {
    call.respondText(call.messages.serverGreeting("Ada"))
}

val german = Messages.forLocale("de").appTitle()
```

Choose how the language is picked with `strategy`:

| Strategy | URLs | Best for | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Cookie` (default) | `/about` | Apps behind a login | Prerendered pages hold the default language and switch on load, so others can flash briefly, and search engines mostly see one language |
| `UrlPrefix` | `/de/about` | Public sites and SEO | Every language gets its own prerendered pages. Plain paths redirect to the visitor's language. Links must use `localizeHref`, or [typed routes](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/routes), or pages won't be prerendered per language |

On the server, `call.svelteLocale` and `call.messages` follow the same rules: the URL prefix if that strategy is on, then the cookie, then `Accept-Language`, then your default. `localizeHref` is safe with either strategy, and `call.localizeHref` does the same for redirects from Ktor.

Parameters are plain text replacements. Plurals and date formatting aren't built in yet.

### Plurals

"1 note" and "2 notes" are one message with two forms, and how many forms there are depends on the language. Write the forms into the message:

```json
{
    "notes-count": "{count, plural, =0 {No notes} one {# note} other {# notes}} in {folder}"
}
```

`#` stands for the number. The generated functions take the count as a number and pick the form for the current language, in TypeScript and in Kotlin alike:

```ts
m.notesCount({ count: notes.length, folder: 'Inbox' });
```

```kotlin
call.messages.notesCount(notes.size, "Inbox")
```

- The forms are `zero`, `one`, `two`, `few`, `many` and `other`. A language uses only some of them: English and German `one` and `other`, Russian and Polish `one`, `few`, `many` and `other`, Japanese only `other`. Every plural needs `other`.
- `=0`, `=1` and so on match one exact number, before the forms of the language. That is how "No notes" is written.
- A form can hold other placeholders, and another plural.
- Counts are whole numbers.
